title: The noble search
hook: the ignoble search chases what ages; the noble search seeks the unaging
carry: worth a search of its own

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bait, and your line, the bait is set. The herd that got away ate without being caught.

Scroll back through a phone's search history. Shoes. Flights. A better job. Is this mole normal. Houses we can't afford. Whether a certain person is still single. It's a strange and honest diary of what we're hunting for, day after day. In MN 26 the Buddha says there are two kinds of search. And he admits, plainly, which kind he once made himself, before his awakening.
screen: `A SEARCH HISTORY IS A DIARY.` → `WHAT ARE WE HUNTING FOR?` → `TWO KINDS OF SEARCH.`

segments.voice: The Ariyapariyesana Sutta is the twenty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. Ariya means noble; pariyesana means search. In the ignoble search, a person who is themselves subject to aging, sickness and death looks for happiness in things that are also subject to aging, sickness and death. He lists them plainly: wife and children, men and women slaves, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, horses, gold and silver. None of these is wicked. The point is only that they age too: you're chasing something that is running out at the same speed you are. In the noble search, a person who sees that they are subject to aging and death looks for what does not age and does not die: the unborn, the deathless, the supreme security from bondage. Buddhists call it nibbana, nirvana in Sanskrit. Then the Buddha tells his own story, in his own voice. Before awakening, he too was making the ignoble search. Then, while still young, black-haired, in the first stage of life, he shaved his head and went forth, though his mother and father wept. He studied with two teachers, Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, mastered what they taught, and left both, because it wasn't yet the end of the search. He walked until he reached a pleasant grove at Uruvela with a clear river, sat down, and there found what he was looking for. So the noble search isn't throwing away the shoes or the house. It's noticing what you're asking them to do. They can't stop you aging. Something else might be worth a search of its own.
screen: `ARIYA: NOBLE · PARIYESANA: SEARCH` · `CHASING WHAT AGES, AS YOU AGE` · `SEEKING THE UNAGING, THE DEATHLESS` · `THE BUDDHA'S OWN SEARCH, TOLD BY HIM` · then, large: `THE NOBLE SEARCH.`

segments.voice: Think of the last three things you searched for, on a screen or in your head, and hold each one lightly: will this age? Then ask what in you was looking underneath, rest, safety, to be loved, and let that deeper wish sit with you as you breathe, without solving it.
ariyapariyesana. A being who ages, seeking what does not age.
Your line: worth a search of its own. Nothing wrong with the shoes; they just can't do that job. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: MN 26 is read as the Buddha's own account of his going forth and awakening, and teachers use its two searches to invite reflection on aging, sickness and death.

original.note: Pali pariyesana: search, seeking. ariyapariyesana: the noble search.

trapdoor: what you thought: a noble search means giving up everything you own.
what it means: it means seeing that what ages can't save you from aging, and looking for what doesn't.
what a scholar hears: MN 26 tells, in the Buddha's own voice, of his going forth, his two teachers (Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta) and his awakening.
recall: a grove; a handful of leaves held up

chat.says: Does the Buddha say wanting a family or a home is wrong?
options: No. They're not wicked; they age too, so they can't be the deathless.
Yes. He called a family and a home wicked things to want.
No. He said they're what the noble search is really for.
chat.meaning: In MN 26 the ignoble search chases what ages; the noble search looks for what doesn't. None of the things listed is wicked: they simply age too.

nibbana.meaning: the unaging, the deathless; nirvana in Sanskrit

Alara Kalama.meaning: one of two teachers the Buddha studied with, then left

Uruvela.meaning: the place by a clear river where the search ended
